mit-college-essay.summary: An MIT admissions officer explains why many college essays sound the same and how to write one that sounds like you: plain words, one real story, no borrowed phrases.
points: Write plainly. Short, direct words beat clever phrases and clichés.
Books of “winning essays” tend to make essays bland. Use them carefully, if at all.
One specific, true story says more than general claims about your goals or character.
Cut anything that does not help the essay.
Imagine telling the story to a relative at dinner, honestly and without trying to impress.
mit-college-essay.note: Archived MIT post from 2012. The advice still holds; check mitadmissions.org for current rules.

mit-applying-sideways.summary: An MIT admissions officer argues that there is no single achievement that gets you in, so stop chasing one. Do well in class, be kind and follow real interests; admission chances follow from that.
points: Take hard classes and learn deeply, because the learning has value whatever happens.
Be kind and help people around you; teachers who write references notice it.
Choose activities you enjoy, not ones picked only to impress a university.
Activities done for appearances often show, and they make your years less happy.

gatech-essay-all-about-you.summary: Georgia Tech's dean of admission tells students to stop guessing what colleges want and write about what they really think and care about, in their own voice.
points: There is no “right” topic. Choose something you actually think about.
Keep your own voice: no forced quotes, no inflated vocabulary.
Use the essay to think about your values and explain them clearly.
AI tools can help you brainstorm, but the final words should be yours.
Too many editors, or paying someone, can erase the voice colleges want to hear.

usc-requesting-teacher-recommendations.summary: A school counsellor writing for USC explains how to ask teachers for recommendation letters that show more than grades, and how to thank them.
points: A teacher from a class where you struggled and improved can write a strong letter.
Follow your school's process and ask early; letters are usually uploaded online.
Recent teachers who know you well are better than teachers from years ago.
Give each teacher a short note: why you chose them, a project you are proud of, anything they should know.
Thank them, and tell them later where you decided to go.

cambridge-interview-what-to-expect.summary: Cambridge's official guide to undergraduate interviews: when they happen, how long they last and what they are like. They are academic conversations about your subject.
points: Everyone who gets an offer has been interviewed, but not everyone interviewed gets an offer.
For 2027 entry the main interviews run from 7 to 18 December 2026; dates usually cannot be moved.
Your college decides whether the interview is online or in person.
Most applicants have one or two interviews, 35 minutes to an hour in total.
Cambridge's guidance is free and it does not endorse paid interview coaching.

harvard-application-tips.summary: Harvard's own walkthrough of the Common App and the Harvard supplement, section by section, with notes on fee waivers, test scores and the short-answer questions.
points: Your application is complete only after the Harvard supplement is submitted.
Use your legal name the same way on every document.
If the fee is a hardship, ask for a waiver; applying for aid does not hurt your chances.
Self-report only official test scores, not practice scores.
Quality of activities matters more than filling every slot; the supplement has five short answers of up to 150 words.

ubc-personal-profile-student-tips.summary: Current UBC students share how they wrote the personal profile, the required short-answer part of the UBC application.
points: List your activities first, then note what you learned from each.
Look for a thread that links your choices and interests.
Draft in a separate document, start early and leave time to revise.
Be honest; small personal stories count.
The profile is one part of the application, next to grades and activities.

ielts-speaking-dont-overdo-it.summary: Official IELTS advice for the Speaking test: be natural, talk about real experiences and do not recite memorised answers.
points: The Speaking test is a face-to-face talk with an examiner, about 15 minutes long.
Made-up stories do not raise your score; real experiences are easier to talk about.
Examiners notice memorised answers.
If your mind goes blank, a phrase like “I'm not sure, but…” still shows good English.
Accents are not marked down. Focus on fluency, grammar and pronunciation.

ielts-10-steps-high-scoring-essays.summary: Official IELTS advice on Writing Task 2: how essays are marked and a simple plan for planning, writing and checking in 40 minutes.
points: Four things are marked equally: answering the task, linking ideas, vocabulary and grammar.
Spend about 5–10 minutes planning, 15–20 writing and 10 checking.
Use a clear shape: introduction, two or three body paragraphs with one idea each, conclusion.
Use linking words only where they help.
In the final check, fix long sentences, repeated words and paragraphs with two ideas.

toefl-common-mistakes.summary: ETS, the maker of the TOEFL iBT, lists eight common mistakes test takers make before and during the test, section by section.
points: General English practice is not enough; learn the TOEFL question types and timing.
Practise each section with a timer.
Learn how the Reading questions work and stay focused in Listening.
Do not memorise Speaking answers; speak at a clear, steady pace.
Use a simple structure in Writing and check grammar and small errors.

duolingo-english-test-prep-guide.summary: The Duolingo English Test team explains how to get ready: know the format, practise English every day and set up a quiet room for test day.
points: The test measures your current English, so cramming the night before changes little.
It is adaptive: questions get harder or easier based on your answers.
Take the free practice test to learn the format and see your likely score range.
On test day you need a quiet, well-lit room, a webcam, a microphone, stable internet and your ID; no headphones.
Results usually arrive within two days.

college-board-digital-sat-tips.summary: College Board's own test-day tips for the digital SAT in Bluebook: pacing, the built-in tools and how to practise.
points: You can show or hide the timer; flag a hard question and come back to it.
Use the annotation tool to highlight and take notes on passages.
Answers have no pattern; use the eliminator to cross out wrong options.
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for guessing.
Take a full practice test in Bluebook, then work on your weakest areas.

usc-submit-test-scores.summary: USC admissions explains how it treats SAT and ACT scores while testing is optional, and how to decide whether to send yours.
points: Sending scores is your choice; send them if you are proud of them.
Your school transcript matters more than test scores.
If you do not send scores, USC does not assume you are hiding something.
If you test more than once, USC uses your best section scores.
usc-submit-test-scores.note: Policies change by year and by university. Check each university's current testing rule.

ucas-choosing-right-uk-course.summary: UCAS's guide for international students applying to UK universities: entry and English requirements, visas, and the new document upload service.
points: Each university sets its own entry requirements, so they differ between courses.
English requirements can differ even between courses at the same university.
You will need a Student visa; the page explains when and how to apply.
For 2027 entry UCAS adds a document upload service, for example for English certificates and passport details.

tufts-college-search-right-fit.summary: Tufts admissions explains what “fit” means and what to think about when choosing where to apply, beyond reputation.
points: Choose for your own goals, not only for a famous name or family pressure.
City, suburb or countryside changes daily life; think about distance from home too.
Large and small universities feel very different.
Research universities and liberal arts colleges have different strengths; check your subject is offered.
Ask current students and admissions staff questions.

jhu-stay-organized-college-search.summary: Johns Hopkins admissions shares simple ways to keep a college search organised: a balanced list, one tracking sheet and tidy email.
points: Apply to about 8–10 universities, mixing reach, target and safer choices.
Name the few things that matter most to you and use them to narrow the list.
Keep one spreadsheet with location, size, deadlines, programmes and student life.
Make an email folder per university and unsubscribe from those you dropped.

usc-faqs-international-families.summary: A USC international admissions officer answers common questions from families abroad about documents, testing, review and money.
points: International applicants send nearly the same materials, plus an English test if needed and translated transcripts.
USC has no country quotas; each application is read on its own.
SAT and ACT are optional, unless you use them to meet the English requirement.
Merit scholarships for international students are limited and have their own deadlines.
USC does not offer need-based aid to international students.

study-in-nl-bachelors.summary: The official Study in NL site explains the two kinds of bachelor's degrees in the Netherlands and how they differ.
points: Universities of applied sciences: usually 4 years (240 credits), practical, with internships.
Research universities: usually 3 years (180 credits), academic, with a thesis.
Degrees include BSc, BA and LLB.
After either one you can work or continue to a master's.

study-australia-understanding-qualificat.summary: Study Australia, the government's site, explains the levels of Australian qualifications and how long each takes.
points: The Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) sets one standard for all levels.
Vocational courses (certificates, diplomas) teach job skills at TAFE and colleges.
A bachelor's degree takes 3–5 years; honours usually adds a year.
You can move up between levels as you study.

waterloo-choosing-career.summary: A University of Waterloo guide for school students on choosing a career: know yourself, define success, research, and do not rush.
points: List your strengths, favourite subjects and tasks you want to avoid.
Decide what success means to you: pay, travel, flexibility or independence.
Check the education needed, salary and daily routine; talk to people in the job.
Co-op programmes let you try a career through paid work during your degree.

ukcisa-opening-bank-account.summary: UKCISA, the UK council for international students, explains which bank accounts students can open in the UK and what checks banks make.
points: Basic bank accounts are usually free and have no overdraft.
Some banks offer international student accounts and Sharia-compliant accounts.
Banks must check your identity and immigration status.
Your university can often give a letter confirming you are a student.
Tell your bank when your address changes or you travel for a long time.

campus-france-where-to-live.summary: Campus France, the French government agency, explains student housing in France, typical rents and how the rental process works.
points: CROUS student residences cost about €450 a month in Paris and €350 elsewhere, but places are scarce.
Private flats start around €800 in Paris and €400 elsewhere.
No French guarantor? The free VISALE guarantee can help; start before you arrive.
The deposit is usually one month's rent. Never pay before you sign a lease.
